raw_case_text:
We report a case of an 87-year-old female patient with a long-standing history of RA. She was undergoing treatment with methotrexate 8 mg/week and monthly injections of the TNF inhibitor golimumab. The patient presented with chief complaints of dyspnea on exertion, dry cough, and fatigue. A month before admission, she started experiencing dry coughing. Three days before presenting to our facility, she experienced a worsening of exertional dyspnea and increased fatigue. Upon initial examination at a local clinic, her oxygen saturation (SpO2) was found to be 70%. A chest X-ray revealed bilateral pulmonary ground-glass opacities. Due to these findings, she was referred to our hospital for further evaluation and treatment.
Upon admission, her vital signs were as follows: pulse 75/min, blood pressure 137/72 mmHg, temperature 36.7 C, respiratory rate 20/min, and SpO2 97% on 3 L/min of supplemental oxygen. Physical examination revealed inspiratory crackles in both lung fields, with no heart murmurs, edema, or joint pain. Her height was 146.0 cm, weight 45.1 kg, and BMI 21.16 kg/m2. In rapid testing, the influenza antigen, SARS-CoV-2 antigen, urinary pneumococcal antigen, and urinary Legionella antigen were all negative. Laboratory findings revealed a WBC count of 13,380/uL, hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL, platelet count 344x103/uL, CRP 20.8 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase level at 478 U/L, D-dimer at 6.6 microg/mL, and KL-6 397 U/mL (reference <500 U/mL). A high-resolution chest CT scan confirmed diffuse, unevenly distributed ground-glass opacities throughout both lungs (Figure 1).
The differential diagnosis included RA-related interstitial lung disease, MTX-induced pneumonitis, and opportunistic infections such as pneumocystis pneumonia, cytomegalovirus pneumonia, and bacterial pneumonia. Treatment was initiated with discontinuation of MTX, administration of steroid pulse therapy (methylprednisolone, or mPSL, 500 mg), trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX), antibiotics (levofloxacin 500 mg/day and ceftriaxone 2 g/day), and supplemental oxygen; 5000 units of Heparin Ca were administered due to elevated D-dimer levels (Figure 2).
On day 3, her respiratory status worsened, necessitating the initiation of high-flow oxygen therapy (Figure 2). On day 6, her serum beta-D-glucan levels on admission were found to be elevated (423 pg/mL). Cytomegalovirus antigen on admission was negative. Considering her clinical background, progression, and imaging findings, she was clinically diagnosed with PCP. Treatment was continued with TMP/SMX (three tablets/day), steroids, and ongoing oxygen supplementation, and antibiotics were discontinued.
On day 12, the patient developed trunk pruritus and rash, prompting a transition from TMP/SMX to atovaquone. On day 19, her chest CT showed complete resolution of the ground-glass opacities (Figure 3), and blood tests indicated decreased inflammatory markers. Steroid treatment was discontinued, and MTX was resumed at a half dose of 4 mg, which had been paused. On day 25, she showed no recurrence of pneumonia and was discharged home in a stable condition.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 87-year-old female with rheumatoid arthritis presented with a 1-month history of dry cough and a 3-day worsening of exertional dyspnea and fatigue.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who had a long-standing history of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) treated with weekly methotrexate (8 mg/week) and monthly golimumab injections, developed a dry cough 1 month prior to admission. Three days prior to hospital referral, her exertional dyspnea and fatigue markedly worsened. At a local clinic, her room-air SpO2 was 70% and a chest X-ray showed bilateral pulmonary ground-glass opacities, prompting urgent referral.
subjective.past_medical_history: Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate (8 mg/week) and monthly golimumab (TNF-alpha inhibitor).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dry cough, exertional dyspnea, and fatigue; negative for arthralgias or peripheral edema. Home medications included methotrexate 8 mg/week and monthly golimumab.

objective.physical_examination: Anthropometrics: Height 146.0 cm, weight 45.1 kg, BMI 21.16 kg/m2. Admission vital signs: Pulse 75/min, blood pressure 137/72 mmHg, temperature 36.7 °C, respiratory rate 20/min, and SpO2 97% on 3 L/min supplemental oxygen (70% at the referring clinic). Chest and systemic exam: Bilateral inspiratory crackles on lung auscultation; no cardiac murmurs, peripheral edema, or joint pain.
objective.routine_investigations: Rapid infectious screening: Negative influenza antigen, SARS-CoV-2 antigen, urinary pneumococcal antigen, urinary Legionella antigen, and serum CMV antigen. Admission blood tests: WBC 13,380/μL, hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL, platelets 344 x 10^3/μL, C-reactive protein (CRP) 20.8 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 478 U/L, D-dimer 6.6 μg/mL, and KL-6 397 U/mL (reference <500 U/mL). Referring clinic chest X-ray: Bilateral pulmonary ground-glass opacities.
objective.advanced_workup: High-resolution chest CT (HRCT) on admission: Diffuse, unevenly distributed ground-glass opacities (GGOs) throughout both lungs. Fungal biomarker (returned on hospital day 6 from admission sample): Markedly elevated serum beta-D-glucan at 423 pg/mL.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) secondary to methotrexate and golimumab immunosuppression for rheumatoid arthritis, clinically confirmed by diffuse bilateral GGOs on HRCT, markedly elevated serum beta-D-glucan (423 pg/mL), elevated LDH (478 U/L), and negative CMV and bacterial antigen screens. Plan and clinical course: Upon admission, methotrexate was discontinued and empiric treatment was initiated with steroid pulse therapy (methylprednisolone 500 mg), trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX), ceftriaxone (2 g/day), levofloxacin (500 mg/day), supplemental oxygen, and subcutaneous heparin calcium (5,000 units for elevated D-dimer). On day 3, worsening hypoxemia required escalation to high-flow nasal cannula oxygen. On day 6, when elevated admission beta-D-glucan (423 pg/mL) and negative CMV antigen confirmed PCP, antibacterials were stopped and TMP/SMX (3 tablets/day) plus corticosteroids were continued. On day 12, she developed truncal pruritus and drug rash, prompting a switch from TMP/SMX to oral atovaquone. By day 19, repeat chest CT showed complete resolution of GGOs with normalized inflammatory markers; steroids were stopped, methotrexate was resumed at a reduced dose (4 mg/week), and she was discharged home in stable condition on day 25.
